newsitem.title: FINLAND: Eurosceptics grab lead in Finnish Europoll.
newsitem.headline: Eurosceptics grab lead in Finnish Europoll.

text.p: Voters in European Union newcomer Finland, following the lead set by Austria, on Sunday sent five prominent Eurosceptics to the European parliament in a clear rebuff to their pro-European government.

With four-fifths of votes counted, two of the country's most outspoken opponents of European integration topped the list of 16 successful candidates in Finland's first direct poll for the Strasbourg-based parliament.
Turnout among Finland's 4.1 million voters was low, at about 61 percent against over 70 percent in the general elections. Analysts said it reflected apathy especially amongst the young.

Current Euro-MP Paavo Vayrynen -- a former foreign minister and the Centre Party's top Eurosceptic -- and Esko Seppanen -- a rogue anti-European member of the governing Left Wing Alliance -- came first and second.

The vote came 22 months after Finland joined the Union with Austria and Sweden, on a referendum in which membership won 57 percent support. But it was the first direct poll for Euro-MPs, who were previously named by parliament.

Coming just a week after Finland linked its currency to Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), a major step towards a single currency, the result underlined popular fears here about Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union.

Only Seppanen made this a major campaign issue, but about 60 percent of Finns have said in opinion polls that they oppose a single currency. Overall, recent opinion polls said less than one-tenth of Finns felt very negative about EU membership.

"I'm an anti-federalist and I've made it clear that I don't want Finland to join EMU. I think the anti-federalist mood of the people was clearly expressed," Seppanen told Reuters, calling a single currency "a short-cut to the federalist state".
"I believe and hope that the government will take seriously the fact that a large portion of the people do not approve of EMU," said opposition leader and former prime minister Esko Aho.

Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen conceded the results showed "a certain amount of... Euroscepticism, or whatever you call it", but denied it was a protest vote. He said Seppanen was "a well-known demagogue" while Vayrynen did not play "a constructive role in our politics".
"It seems that the ERM-link, which we had to do, has had an effect," commented Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto.
Government ministers had argued the link had to be made to give parliament a choice when it comes to deciding on EMU.
"The EMU train has left and the only alternative for the government is to act as if EMU will take off in 1999," Lipponen said.

The election, held concurrently with municipal elections, showed a clear swing towards Aho's Centre Party, which grabbed 25.7 percent of the vote with 79.1 percent of votes counted. This was up from 19.8 percent in general elections in 1995.

Lipponen's Social Democrats (SDP), who lead the coalition, saw their share fall to 21.5 percent from 28.3 percent in the last national poll. The swing was less marked in the municipal poll, with the SDP holding a slim lead.

"You are going to see a major change in the political map of Finland as a result of these elections," Centre Party leader Aho told reporters as results came through. He called the shift in his party's favour "staggering".

However, unlike last week's Austrian Europoll, the results left the distribution of Finland's seats at Strasbourg unchanged. The Centre Party had led the coalition that took Finland into Europe in 1995 and already had the biggest mandate with five seats.
